title: In Raphael’s School of Athens, every receding line meets between Plato and Aristotle
body: Raphael painted [The School of Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_School_of_Athens) in 1509–1511 for Pope Julius II, on a wall of the Stanza della Segnatura in the Vatican Palace; the fresco is about 7.7 m wide and 5 m high. Its hall is drawn in **one-point perspective**: every edge that runs straight back from us, the cornices, the vaults and the lines of the floor, aims at a single vanishing point between Plato and Aristotle, about half a metre below Aristotle’s outstretched hand by one measurement. That point sits at the painter’s eye height, and a level line through it is the horizon. The floor also gives the distance: if its tiles are square, their diagonals meet on the horizon at two **distance points**, and their gap from the vanishing point is how far back the eye stood. [Christopher Tyler and Michael Kubovy](https://webexhibits.org/sciartperspective/raphaelperspective4.html) reconstruct about 9 m, with the horizon at least 4 m above the floor, in a room only about 8 m long. They suggest Raphael meant it: the fresco starts 2 m up, so drawn for a visitor’s real eye, none of its floor would show.

slides.prompt: Raphael built The School of Athens around one spot for the viewer’s eye. Can a visitor in the room stand there?
slides.answer: No: it is about 9 m out, behind the opposite wall
slides.detail: Christopher Tyler and Michael Kubovy worked this out from the floor tiles, assuming they are square. The room is only about 8 m long, and the eye is at least 4 m up.

slides.alt: Animation on dark slate: a schematic of Raphael's School of Athens. Red construction lines along the painted hall's edges meet at a gold vanishing point between Plato and Aristotle; a horizon at the eye height; tile diagonals run to two distance points 9 m away; the eye lands behind the far wall.
slides.music: “Prelude in C (BWV 846)” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Drag the point until every receding edge runs through it. Then switch to the distance point and find where the tiles’ diagonals meet the horizon.
slides.takeaway: The edges meet at the eye height, 4.2 m up in this model, and the tile diagonals meet the horizon 9 m to the side, so the eye was 9 m back. In the real room, that spot is behind the opposite wall.

slides.alt: Looking up at The School of Athens on its wall in the Vatican: Plato in red and Aristotle in blue stand under receding arches at the centre of the fresco, with the painted vault of the room above.
slides.caption: Plato (red) and Aristotle (blue) stand where the painted hall’s lines converge.

slides.heading: Reading the painter’s eye off a picture

steps.label: Extend the edges that run straight back
They meet at the vanishing point
A level line through it is the eye height
Square tiles’ diagonals give distance points
Their gap from it is the viewing distance

slides.heading: Where the eye should be, and where it is

left.label: The perspective’s eye
left.text: About 9 m from the wall and at least 4 m above the floor, by Tyler and Kubovy’s reconstruction.

right.label: A visitor
right.text: Standing on the floor of a room about 8 m long, well below the horizon. The painted floor looks tilted, yet still leads the eye in.

slides.question: In The School of Athens, what do the diagonals of the square floor tiles tell you?
options: How far back the painter’s eye was
How big the real room is
slides.explanation: The tiles’ diagonals meet on the horizon at two distance points; their gap from the vanishing point is the viewing distance. The vanishing point itself gives the eye height.

source.label: Tyler & Kubovy: The Rise of Renaissance Perspective (WebExhibits)
